extracted.intended_audience: general readers, social reformers, public-health and housing policymakers interested in urban tenement conditions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for understanding, distinguishing, and judging living conditions, health risks, social behaviour, and policy responses in urban tenements (late 19th-century New York). Focuses on physical markers of housing quality, causes of morbidity/mortality, behavioural effects of poverty, and remedial measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing a 'flat' from a tenement
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'flat' is indicated by features that secure privacy (locked door, door-bell); the absence of these (open halls used as highways by all) marks a tenement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "A locked door is a strong point in favor of the flat. ... But never a 'flat' without it. The hall that is a highway for all the world by night and by day is the tenement's proper badge." Use presence of privacy features (locked door, bell, private hall) as practical criteria when classifying housing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of saloons as a neighbourhood respectability guide
rubrics_metrics.description: The count of saloons on a corner or in a block serves as an indicator of the neighbourhood's character: few saloons suggests a more 'respectable' tenement neighbourhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The fact that there are not more than two saloons on the corner, nor over three or four in the block will serve as a fair guide." Use saloon density alongside other signs to assess social environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local industry determines tenement character
rubrics_metrics.description: The kind of work carried on in a locality (docks, gas-houses, slaughter-houses, big workshops) largely determines the tenement character, attracting rough crowds and vilest saloons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Areas near heavy industry and docks are more likely to be slum-centres; use local employment patterns as a predictive factor for housing and social conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of rear houses, winding passages, and 'runways' as slum features
rubrics_metrics.description: Clusters of rear houses, odd winding passages or no passages (only runways for thieves and toughs) indicate the worst tenement conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical layout—many rear houses on a lot, labyrinthine yards, and lack of clear passages—serve as red flags for dangerously overcrowded or criminally-inclined tenement blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green space and private gardens as stabilising influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Gardens, small parks, and private shrubbery in tenement districts improve order and reduce disorder and agitation among residents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the German immigrant's love of flowers improves neighbourhood order; converting Tompkins Square into a park ended the Bread and Blood riots. Policy implication: small parks system relieves congestion and reduces social disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summer overcrowding hazards (rooftop sleeping and hot-weather mortality)
rubrics_metrics.description: In hot months tenement residents sleep on roofs, fire-escapes, trucks and crowded outdoor spaces; this leads to accidents (falls) and heightened mortality among infants and children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for increased deaths by rolling off roofs/window-sills in June–August and plan interventions (cooling, shelter, water supply, medical visits). The text cites police reports and the need for targeted summer measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epidemic vulnerability due to inability to isolate
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowding in tenements makes it practically impossible to isolate contagious patients, causing ordinarily mild diseases (measles, grippe) to become frequently fatal among poor children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health response: use health officers' powers to remove dangerous cases to hospitals; provide summer doctors, nursing, and fresh-air excursions to reduce mortality. Death-maps reveal tightly defined epidemic tracks through crowded blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary reform and building standards reduce death-rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Taller modern tenements built under sanitary-reform rules show lower death-rates compared to older houses converted into tenements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "As the buildings grew taller the death-rate fell." New construction meeting sanitary laws reduces mortality; old converted houses are indicated as irredeemable without demolition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance, poverty, and poor hygienic surroundings as mortality factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance combined with poverty and bad hygiene causes starvation, neglect of treatable disease, and preventable deaths (examples: peritonitis, lead-poisoned laborer, contagious eye disease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess household income, parental illness/disability, and access to food/medical care when evaluating risk; charitable relief and medical visits can sometimes only alleviate temporarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic precarity and instalment-driven improvidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Living from hand to mouth produces dependence on instalment plans and short-term consumption that discourages saving and planning, reinforcing improvidence and wasteful spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instalment purchasing and immediate consumption (including expensive funerals) are predictable behaviours under chronic low wages; policy interventions should address insecure earnings and provide alternatives to high-cost credit/consumption patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funeral extravagance as a culturally embedded waste in poverty
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of expensive funerals and wakes is common among tenement populations and can consume lifetime savings, deepening family want after a death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize cultural importance of funerals but note the economic harm; social critics and clergy denounce the practice, but it persists due to social/political incentives (e.g., 'show of strength').

rubrics_metrics.name: Water scarcity in summer encourages drunkenness
rubrics_metrics.description: Scarcity of water during hot weather encourages the poor to seek relief in alcohol, contributing significantly to intemperance-related problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public utilities and potable water provision are public-health and moral issues; ensuring water access in summer is a preventive measure against increased drunkenness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of causation between intemperance and distress
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a two-way relationship: intemperance may cause distress, but distress (poverty, overcrowding) also causes intemperance; the Society for Improving the Condition of the Poor attributes ~40% of cases to one or the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing social ills, consider both directions of causation and avoid simplistic attribution solely to moral failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal protection and actual eviction frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite common belief, evictions are less frequent than reported because civil courts and elected judges often favor tenants (the 'Poor Man's Court'); many dispossession warrants do not result in actual evictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use court-process data cautiously: high numbers of dispossess warrants do not equal evictions. Political factors (tenant voters) affect judicial outcomes; this has implications for housing policy and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community solidarity as a coping mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenement communities habitually share scarce resources; neighbours who are almost as poor often help those worse off, a moral virtue of the tenements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating social capital in slums, account for informal mutual-aid networks that can offset some harms and are a potential basis for community-based interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child population density and school capacity mismatch
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme concentration of children in single houses (e.g., 170 children in one building) overwhelms school capacity; thousands of poor children are crowded out of schools yearly for lack of room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use household child counts and school-room availability as joint metrics to assess educational neglect risk and to prioritise expansion of schooling and truancy outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenement architecture and layout as irreversible vs improvable
rubrics_metrics.description: Newer tenements built under sanitary reforms are improvable and have better mortality outcomes; old houses converted into tenements are structurally deficient and can only be adequately remedied by demolition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess buildings by date and conformity to sanitary laws to decide on remediation vs demolition; policy choices should prioritize replacing irredeemable stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black-and-tan saloon as marker of moral depravity (author's depiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'black-and-tan' saloon (where white and black races meet in debauch) is described as the worst form of commingling, gathering law-breakers and human wrecks and fostering violent incidents with razors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats certain mixed-race dives as concentrated loci of crime and violence; as an evaluator, consider such establishments indicators of extreme social disorder—note the author's moralizing language and the historical/racial framing of the observation.
